title: Final contest: prefix sums, decoding, counting subsequences
overview: The course's final contest. The problems reward quick pattern spotting: prefix sums for range queries, a two-step string walk for decoding, a counting argument for the missing pair, a closed formula for a repeating sequence, a frequency structure for 'most common value' queries, and a small DP that counts subsequences. Two files hold only the statement, so their notes describe the approach.

concepts.explain: `pre[i]` = sum of the first i values. The sum of positions L..R is `pre[R] - pre[L-1]`, so each query is O(1) after O(N) setup.
concepts.snippet:
pre[i] = pre[i-1] + a[i];
ans = pre[R] - pre[L-1];

concepts.term: Counting pairs with a fixed sum
concepts.explain: Two non-negative numbers adding up to S can be chosen in S + 1 ordered ways: (0, S), (1, S-1), ..., (S, 0).
When N is up to 10^9 you cannot build the sequence. Write a function for the sum of its first x elements and answer ranges with f(R) - f(L-1).
To repeatedly find the value with the highest count (ties: largest value), keep `map<value, count>` and a `set<pair<count, value>>`; the last element of the set is the answer.
`dp[i][j]` = ways the first j letters of the pattern appear as a subsequence in the first i letters of the text. Either skip text letter i, or, if it matches, also use it.

concepts.term: Big local arrays overflow the stack
concepts.explain: A local array of a million `long long` needs 8 MB, more than the default stack. Make big arrays global or `static`.

files.title: Magical Forest Fruits (prefix sums)
files.what: Answers range-sum queries with a prefix-sum array.
steps: Read `N`, `Q` and the fruits into `fruits[1..N]` (global array).
Build `sum[i] = sum[i-1] + fruits[i]`.
For each query print `sum[R] - sum[L-1]`.
files.input_note: N Q, the N counts, then Q lines `L R` (1-based). This is the contest sample.
files.output_note: `7`, `13` and `5`, matching the sample: each line is `sum[R] - sum[L-1]`.
files.watch_out: `long long sum[1000005]` is declared inside `main`: about 8 MB of stack (fine on judges with a big stack, a crash on a default 1 MB stack). It is also never zeroed, so `sum[0]` is garbage in principle; the output is right here only because that memory happened to be 0. Fix: make `sum` a global next to `fruits` (globals start at 0).

check.q: Using the sample, what is the sum for query `3 5`?

files.title: String Decoder
files.what: Walks the encoded string two characters at a time: a letter, then a digit telling how many copies to append.
steps: `freq = s[i+1] - '0'` turns the digit character into a number.
Append `s[i]` to `ans` `freq` times (zero times for 0).
Print `ans` for each test case.
files.complexity: Time O(|S| + output length) · Space O(output length)
files.input_note: T, then T encoded strings. This is the contest sample.
files.output_note: Prints `aabbbc` and `xzz`, matching the sample; `y0` disappears.

check.a: Digit characters have consecutive character codes, so subtracting the code of '0' gives the digit's value.

files.title: Array Reconstruction (counting pairs)
files.what: The two missing values must add up to `original_sum - (sum of the remaining values)`. If that is S, there are S + 1 ordered pairs of non-negative numbers.
steps: `possible_ways(n)` reads the n-2 remaining values and adds them up.
Read the original sum.
`S = original_sum - remaining_sum`.
Return `S + 1`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per test · Space O(n)
files.input_note: t; each test: n, the n-2 remaining values, the original sum. The first test is from the statement.
files.watch_out: Use `long long`: the sum can be 10^18. The array `rest` is not needed; a running total is enough.

check.q: Remaining values sum to 10 and the original sum is 10. How many ways?

files.title: Pain Sum (statement only)
files.what: The sequence is 1,1,1,2,2,2,3,3,3,... of length N (up to 10^9). Range sums must come from a formula. The file contains only the problem statement.
steps: Define `f(x)` = sum of the first x elements.
Let `q = x / 3` (complete triples) and `r = x % 3` (leftover positions).
The complete triples give `3 * q * (q + 1) / 2`; the leftovers each equal `q + 1`, adding `r * (q + 1)`.
Answer each query with `f(R) - f(L-1)` in `long long`.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per query · Space O(1)
files.input_note: The file has no code, so nothing runs.
files.output_note: No output. Check with the sample (N = 9): f(9) = 18, f(1) = 1, f(6) = 9, so the queries give 17, 8 and 9.
files.watch_out: Only the statement was saved; there is no solution in this file. q can reach about 3x10^8, so `q * (q + 1)` needs `long long`.

files.title: Max (statement only)
files.what: Add values, and on query 2 print the most frequent value (largest on ties), then remove max(1, count/2) copies of it. The file contains only the problem statement.
steps: Keep `map<int, long long> cnt` and `set<pair<long long, int>> best` holding (count, value).
Add X: erase the old pair `(cnt[X], X)` if present, increase `cnt[X]`, insert the new pair.
Query 2: if `best` is empty print `empty`; otherwise the last element `prev(best.end())` is (highest count, largest value).
Print the value, remove `max(1, count / 2)` copies, and re-insert the pair if the count is still above 0.
Use fast I/O and `"\n"`, as the statement asks.
files.complexity: Time O(log n) per query · Space O(n)
files.input_note: The file has no code, so nothing runs.
files.output_note: No output. On the sample the plan prints `empty`, then `12` (12 and 10 both have 4 copies; 12 is larger, two copies removed), then `10` (now 10 has 4 copies and 12 has 2).
files.watch_out: Only the statement was saved; there is no solution in this file. A `priority_queue` alone cannot update counts; the set of pairs (or lazy deletion) is needed.

check.q: Why do pairs `(count, value)` in a set give the right tie-break?
check.a: Pairs are ordered by count first, then by value, so the last pair has the highest count and, among equal counts, the largest value.

files.title: Help Hablu!!! (count subsequences)
files.what: Counts how many times the 3-letter pattern `t` occurs as a subsequence of `s`, with a DP table `arr[i][j]`.
steps: `arr[i][0] = 1` for every i: the empty pattern appears once in any prefix.
For each text position `i` and pattern length `j` (1..3), start with `arr[i-1][j]` (skip `s[i-1]`).
If `s[i-1] == t[j-1]`, add `arr[i-1][j-1]` (use this letter as the j-th pattern letter).
The answer is `arr[n][3]`, stored in `long long`.
files.complexity: Time O(|s|) per test · Space O(|s|)
files.input_note: T; each test: s, then t. Two cases from the contest sample (expected 6 and 11).
files.watch_out: `long long arr[n+1][4]` is a local array; with |s| = 3x10^5 it takes about 9.6 MB of stack and may crash. Only the previous row is needed, so four `long long` counters are enough.

check.q: How many times does `ab` occur as a subsequence of `aabb`?
check.a: 4: each of the two a's pairs with each of the two b's.

files.title: Static Range Sum Queries (practice)
files.what: Answers q questions of the form 'what is the sum of the values from position a to position b?' on an array that never changes. The plain prefix sum this contest keeps asking for, in its simplest form.
steps: Build `pre` of size n+1 with `pre[0] = 0` and `pre[i] = pre[i-1] + value[i]`, so `pre[i]` is the sum of the first i values.
A query a..b is then `pre[b] - pre[a-1]`: the whole prefix up to b, minus the part before a.
`pre[0] = 0` is why a query starting at position 1 needs no special case; `pre[1-1]` is simply 0.
`pre` is `long long`: 2 * 10^5 values of up to 10^9 add up past what an int holds.
`ios::sync_with_stdio(false)` and `cin.tie(nullptr)`, and `"\n"` instead of `endl`, because 2 * 10^5 queries of slow I/O is what makes this problem time out.
files.input_note: n and q, then the n values, then q lines `a b` with 1-based positions.
files.output_note: Prints `11`, `2`, `24`, `4`, one per line. The prefix sums are 3, 5, 9, 14, 15, 16, 21, 24, so query 2..4 is 14 - 3 = 11 and query 3..3 is 9 - 5 = 4.
files.watch_out: The positions are 1-based and both ends are included, so it is `pre[b] - pre[a-1]`, not `pre[b] - pre[a]`. Writing `pre[b] - pre[a]` silently drops the value at position a.

check.q: What does this print for the query `1 1` on the sample array?

files.title: Distinct Subsequences (practice)
files.what: Counts how many different ways the string `t` can be picked out of `s` as a subsequence. Two ways differ when they use different positions of `s`, even if the letters look the same. It is the LCS table of Module 18 with `+` where LCS takes a `max`.
steps: `dp[i][j]` = the number of ways to build the first j letters of t out of the first i letters of s.
`dp[i][0] = 1` for every i: the empty t is built in exactly one way, by taking nothing.
Row 0 stays 0 for j > 0: a non-empty t cannot come out of an empty s.
`dp[i][j]` always includes `dp[i-1][j]`, the ways that leave `s[i-1]` out.
If `s[i-1] == t[j-1]`, add `dp[i-1][j-1]` as well: the ways that use this letter as `t[j-1]`, with both strings stepping back one.
The answer is `dp[n][m]`. The table is `long long` because a half-built count can grow past an int even when the final answer fits.
files.complexity: Time O(n * m) · Space O(n * m)
files.input_note: s on the first line, t on the second. The first sample of the problem.
files.output_note: Prints `numDistinct = 3`: `rabbit` comes out of `rabbbit` by dropping any one of the three b's. On `babgbag\nbag\n` it prints `numDistinct = 5`.
files.watch_out: Counting, not matching: when the letters agree you still add `dp[i-1][j]`, because skipping that letter of s is a different set of choices that may also spell t. Dropping that term counts only some of the ways.

check.q: Why is `dp[i][0]` set to 1 and not 0?
check.a: There is exactly one way to build the empty string out of any prefix of s: pick no letters at all. Zero there would make the whole table zero.

recap: Many range-sum queries: build prefix sums once.
Huge N: find a formula for the prefix sum instead of building the array.
Pairs of non-negative numbers with sum S: S + 1 ways.
Frequency questions with updates: map for counts + set of (count, value).
Counting subsequences: skip the letter, or use it if it matches, and add.
Keep big arrays global; the stack is small.

check_yourself.a: So that a query starting at L = 1 works: `pre[R] - pre[0]` must equal the sum of the first R values.

check_yourself.q: In the subsequence DP, why add `dp[i-1][j-1]` only when the letters match?
check_yourself.a: Only a matching letter can serve as the j-th letter of the pattern; the ways to form the first j-1 letters before it are exactly `dp[i-1][j-1]`.

check_yourself.q: Would a 10^6-element `int` array inside `main` be safe?
check_yourself.a: Usually not: it needs about 4 MB, while the default stack is often 1 MB (Windows) to 8 MB. Make it global.

body: This is the last contest of the course, and it rewards the same habit as the mock: spend the first minute on the limits, not on the story.

Take a question you can picture. Someone hands you a row of numbers and then asks, again and again, "what do positions L to R add up to?". If the row has a million numbers and there are a hundred thousand questions, the honest answer - loop from L to R for each question - is 10^11 steps. That is far beyond the second you are given. The limits said so before you started.
The fix is the oldest trick in the course: do the work once, in advance. Build `pre[i]` = the sum of the first `i` numbers, and every question becomes one subtraction.

Why `pre[0] = 0` matters: a question starting at position 1 needs `pre[R] - pre[0]`, so that slot must hold the sum of nothing. Setting it up costs one pass, and each question then costs one step instead of a million.

What is new compared with the earlier modules is not the tool - you have had prefix sums since Data Structures Module 3. What is new is that nobody tells you which tool it is. The statement says "enchanted fruits" and you have to hear "range sum".

**A second angle on the same idea.** Sometimes you cannot build the array at all, because the row is a billion long. If it follows a rule, that rule gives a formula for the prefix sum and you store nothing. For the row 1, 2, 3, 4, ... the sum of the first `x` values is `x * (x + 1) / 2`, so positions 5 to 9 add up to 45 - 10 = 35. Same subtraction, no array. Whenever `N` reaches 10^9, this is the shape the problem wants.

**A third angle: count on paper before you code.** "In how many ways can two numbers that are 0 or more add up to 4?" Write them out: (0,4), (1,3), (2,2), (3,1), (4,0). Five - that is S + 1 for a sum of S. A question that looks like a search turns into one line of arithmetic, and that is usually the intended solution when the numbers go up to 10^18.

Two more shapes appear here. A string that has to be *decoded* is usually a plain walk with a small state: step through the characters and decide at each step what to append. Remember that `'7'` is a character, not the number 7; `'7' - '0'` gives you the number.

And "how many times does this short pattern appear as a subsequence?" is a small DP. Count `ab` inside `aabb` by hand: each of the two `a`s can pair with each of the two `b`s, so 4. The table version says the same thing - at each letter of the text you either skip it, or, when it matches, also use it and add the ways of building the shorter pattern before it.

Three things cost marks here more than anything else. Totals in these problems reach 10^18, so `int` is not enough; use `long long`. Big arrays must be global or `static`, because a local array of a million `long long` asks for 8 MB and the stack usually has 1 MB. And with many test cases, clear your arrays and counters between them, or the previous answer leaks into the next.
The six entries below go through the problems one at a time. Four have solutions to read; two kept only the statement, so their notes set out the plan you would have written.
